passages.t: The Valley of Vision: walls and water, but no look to God
passages.happening:
‘This is the burden against the Valley of Vision’ (verse 1). Why have the people all gone up to the rooftops, a city full of commotion and revelry (verses 1-2)? Their dead did not die in battle. Their rulers fled together and were captured without a bow being drawn (verses 2-3).

The prophet will not be comforted: ‘Turn away from me, let me weep bitterly’ (verse 4). The Lord GOD of Hosts has set a day of tumult and trampling in the Valley of Vision (verse 5). Elam and Kir come armed, and the valleys fill with chariots (verses 6-7).

The people look to the weapons in the House of the Forest (verse 8). They inspect the breaches in the walls, collect water from the lower pool, count the houses and tear them down to strengthen the wall, and build a reservoir between the walls (verses 9-11). ‘But you did not look to the One who made it, or consider Him who planned it long ago’ (verse 11).

On that day God called for weeping and sackcloth (verse 12). Instead there is feasting, cattle slaughtered and wine poured: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!” (verse 13). The LORD says, ‘Until your dying day, this sin of yours will never be atoned for’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Every oracle so far has been aimed at a foreign nation. Now, with no warning, the heading reads the Valley of Vision, and the target is Jerusalem. God's own city stands under the same judgment as Babylon, Moab and Egypt when it trusts in the same things.

The crisis is most often linked to Sennacherib's invasion in 701 BC. As the Assyrians ravaged Judah's towns, Hezekiah strengthened Jerusalem's defenses, and Scripture and archaeology both preserve the details. The House of the Forest was the great hall Solomon built with cedar pillars and used as an armory. Hezekiah blocked springs outside the city and brought water inside through a tunnel cut through bedrock from the Gihon spring to the Pool of Siloam; an inscription describing its cutting was found in it in 1880. In the 1970s archaeologists in Jerusalem uncovered a massive wall from this period, often called the Broad Wall, built across the foundations of houses that had been torn down to make way for it, just as verse 10 describes. Some scholars instead link verses 1 to 14 to the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, when King Zedekiah and his officials fled and were captured, which fits verse 3 closely.

Isaiah does not condemn the walls or the water. He condemns doing all of it without looking to God. The cheering on the rooftops may reflect the relief when Sennacherib withdrew. God had called for repentance, and the city threw a party.
passages.later: Chronicles records how Hezekiah's men ‘stopped up all the springs and the stream that flowed through the land’ (2 Chronicles 32:4). And Paul quotes the feasters' slogan: if the dead are not raised, ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die’ (1 Corinthians 15:32).
passages.hard:
What does verse 14 mean when it says this sin will never be atoned for until they die?

The line is severe, and readers have asked whether it describes an unforgivable sin. Most interpreters read it in its setting. The sin is the city's refusal to repent when God plainly called for mourning, choosing instead a defiant feast and a fatalistic slogan. Until your dying day may mean that the guilt remains as long as the people keep that attitude, or that the judgment it brings will not be lifted in their lifetime. The Old Testament speaks of sins for which no sacrifice was provided, especially deliberate, defiant sins (Numbers 15:30-31).

This is not a statement that God refuses anyone who later repents. Isaiah is full of invitations to turn back: ‘let him return to the LORD, that He may have compassion, and to our God, for He will freely pardon’ (55:7). It is a warning that hardening the heart against a direct call to repentance has consequences that cannot be bargained away. No reader who is afraid they have gone too far should hear this verse as a door shut on them.
passages.asks: Jerusalem did everything a careful city should do and never looked to God. Ask where you are planning well and praying little. And ask whether you have answered a call to grief with a party.

passages.t: Shebna's tomb, and the key of the house of David
passages.happening:
The Lord sends Isaiah to Shebna, the steward in charge of the palace (verse 15). What is he doing, carving a tomb for himself high in the rock (verse 16)? The LORD is about to shake him, roll him into a ball and sling him into a wide land, where he will die with his glorious chariots, a disgrace to his master's house (verses 17-18). He will be removed from office (verse 19).

‘On that day I will summon My servant, Eliakim son of Hilkiah’ (verse 20). God will clothe him with Shebna's robe and sash and give him his authority, ‘and he will be a father to the dwellers of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah’ (verse 21). ‘I will place on his shoulder the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open’ (verse 22). He will be like a peg driven into a firm place, a throne of honor for his father's house (verse 23).

But his family will hang all their weight on him, every bowl and jar (verse 24), and in that day the peg will give way and fall, and the load on it will be cut down (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Shebna held the office of steward over the palace, the chief minister of the kingdom. In chapters 36 and 37, Eliakim holds that office and Shebna appears as secretary, which suggests the demotion announced here. A burial inscription found in the village of Silwan, across the Kidron Valley from Jerusalem, belongs to a royal steward whose name ends in yahu; some scholars suggest it was Shebna's tomb.

A grand rock-cut tomb was a way for an official to make a lasting name for himself. Shebna was building a monument while the city faced disaster.

The key on the shoulder was a sign of the steward's authority: he controlled who could enter the king's house and who could not. A peg driven into a wall held whatever was hung on it. Eliakim is a good man, a father to the people. But even he cannot bear the whole weight of his family's hopes. When everything is hung on one man, the peg will give way. The first hearers were being warned not to put their trust even in good officials.
passages.later: Isaiah later names both men at the siege: ‘Eliakim son of Hilkiah the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder’ (Isaiah 36:3). And the risen Christ speaks to the church in Philadelphia as the one ‘who holds the key of David. What He opens no one can shut, and what He shuts no one can open’ (Revelation 3:7).
passages.asks: Shebna carved a tomb for his own name, and Eliakim was given a key for the sake of others. Ask what you are building for your own name. And ask on whom you are hanging all your weight, and whether that peg can bear it.
